topic: Starship Flight 14 flew less than half full and still carried about ten times a Falcon 9 launch's Starlink capacity

through_line.name: the stack of flat satellites
through_line.progression: a short stack of small satellites on the slim rocket, then a half-filled bay of big flat satellites, then a bay packed to the top
through_line.resolution: the packed stack fans out into orbit and the loop returns to the half-full bay

blocks.vo_line: Starship flew less than half full. It still carried about ten times the internet capacity of a Falcon 9 launch.
blocks.through_line_state: half-filled bay of big flat satellites beside the slim rocket's tiny stack
shots: MEDIUM, slow push-in: the huge steel ship glides over the curved planet and its payload door swings open with a clunk
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: inside the open door a half-filled stack of big flat satellites, empty slots glowing above it
WIDE, gentle drift: the slim white rocket floats beside the steel ship, its tiny stack of small satellites dwarfed
CLOSE-UP, low angle: the first flat satellite slides out and snaps its solar wing open
OVERHEAD, whip: a row of flat satellites fans out into orbit and settles into a glowing line

blocks.vo_line: On September twenty-eighth, SpaceX's Flight 14 reached orbit for the first time and released twenty-six new Starlink V3 internet satellites.
blocks.through_line_state: the half-filled stack rides up inside the steel ship
shots: WIDE, static: the steel ship stands on the seaside pad at dawn, steam rolling across the ground
CLOSE-UP, low angle: the engine ring ignites in a bright orange burst, the pad shakes
MEDIUM, crane up: the ship lifts off and climbs past the tower on a thick column of flame
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: a counter ring of twenty-six small lights clicks on one by one on the stacked satellites
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, slow push-in: the ship arcs over the horizon and the sky darkens into space

blocks.vo_line: Each V3 is designed for about one terabit per second of downlink. SpaceX says that's more than ten times an older V2 Mini.
blocks.through_line_state: one big flat satellite lifted out of the half-filled stack for inspection
shots: WIDE, static: inside the bright payload bay a mechanical arm lifts one big flat satellite off the stack
CLOSE-UP, orbit: the flat satellite rotates, a fat beam of blue light pours from its underside
MEDIUM, static: a small older satellite with two narrow wings drops in beside it with a bounce
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, push-in: the small satellite's thin beam flickers next to the big satellite's wide beam
LOW ANGLE MEDIUM, static: ten thin beams stack up and finally match the single wide beam, landing with a stamp

blocks.vo_line: A Falcon 9 carries up to about twenty-nine of those smaller V2 Minis, adding only a few terabits per launch.
blocks.through_line_state: the slim rocket's short stack of small satellites
shots: WIDE, gentle drift: the slim white rocket's upper stage coasts along the glowing edge of the planet
CLOSE-UP, static: its nose cover splits and falls away with a pop, revealing a short stack of small satellites
MEDIUM, slow push-in: the small satellites peel off one after another like cards from a deck
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: three thin blue beams switch on and point down at the planet
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, crane pull-back: the little cluster looks tiny against the huge planet below

blocks.vo_line: So Flight 14's satellites add up to roughly twenty-six terabits. At full capacity, Starship is designed to carry sixty of them.
blocks.through_line_state: the stack grows from half full to packed to the ceiling
shots: CLOSE-UP, static: twenty-six flat satellites sit stacked halfway up the bay wall, each glowing softly
WIDE, crane up: more flat satellites drop onto the stack one after another until it nearly touches the ceiling
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, push-in: the final satellite slots into the top of the stack with a satisfying clunk
MEDIUM, orbit: the packed stack glows brighter as all its lights turn on together
LOW ANGLE WIDE, static: the payload door closes over the full stack and settles shut

blocks.vo_line: It wasn't flawless. The ship lost an engine on the way up, and SpaceX brought it down early, about three hours after liftoff.
blocks.through_line_state: the emptied bay after the satellites are gone
shots: CLOSE-UP, static: one engine in the ring sputters and goes dark with a puff of smoke
WIDE, gentle drift: the steel ship tilts and starts a slow fall back toward a bright blue ocean
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: a cartoon clock face on the ship's side spins forward three hours
MEDIUM, low angle: the ship glows as it drops through fluffy clouds, flaps waving
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, slow push-in: the ship hovers low over the waves just before touching the water

blocks.vo_line: It exploded after splashing down. But roughly ten times the capacity per launch changes how fast the whole network can grow.
blocks.through_line_state: the released satellites multiply into a web around the planet
shots: WIDE, static: far out on the ocean a cartoon splash erupts into a puffy orange cloud
MEDIUM, orbit: the planet turns as flat satellites take their places in neat rings
CLOSE-UP, static: glowing links snap between neighbouring satellites, one after another
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, push-in: a tiny house on the planet lights up as a beam reaches it
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, crane pull-back: the whole planet is wrapped in a bright woven web of links

blocks.vo_line: Fully loaded, that's about sixty terabits per launch. SpaceX says more than twenty times a Falcon 9. Which is wild, because
blocks.through_line_state: the packed stack beside the slim rocket's tiny stack, then back to the half-filled bay
shots: MEDIUM, gentle drift: the steel ship's door opens on a stack packed to the top
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: sixty glowing lights blink on down the full stack
WIDE, slow push-in: the slim white rocket's tiny stack floats beside the huge full stack for scale
CLOSE-UP, low angle: the full stack fans out in a long sweeping ribbon of satellites
OVERHEAD, static: the door eases back to a half-filled stack, settling into the opening view
